Dataflow: The untrusted user-controlled input 'query' is passed directly as a string to the database executeQuery method without parameterization. Sanitization: No sanitization or parameterization is applied to the input. This is a intentional SQL injection vulnerability provided as a teaching exercise in the WebGoat project.

title: datadog/java-sqli
message: Source: The 'column' parameter provided via @RequestParam. Sink: Line 54, where the 'column' parameter is directly concatenated into the SQL statement string. Dataflow: Untrusted input flows from the controller parameter directly into the SQL query construction. Sanitization: No allowlisting, validation, or escaping of the 'column' parameter is performed. Since PreparedStatement cannot parameterize ORDER BY identifiers, this allows for SQL injection. Conclusion: Confirmed as a true positive.

title: datadog/java-xpathi
message: Source: User-provided input 'editor' from the request parameter. Sink: The application uses 'compiler.getTask' (line 98) followed by 'task.call()' (line 99) to compile and execute user-supplied Java code. Dataflow: The user input is concatenated into a raw string representing a Java class at lines 105-110, then passed to the Java compiler API. Sanitization: No effective sanitization is performed to prevent arbitrary code execution before compilation. This is a clear case of dynamic code execution on the server.

title: datadog/java-xss
message: Source: The 'query' request parameter from the user. Sink: statement.executeQuery(query) on line 49. Dataflow: The user-provided 'query' string is passed directly into a JDBC Statement executeQuery method without any sanitization, parameterization, or validation. Sanitization: None. This is a classic SQL Injection vulnerability in a known vulnerable educational context.

title: datadog/java-cmdi
message: Source: The 'taskAction' field is populated via deserialization in 'readObject' using 'stream.defaultReadObject()'. Sink: Runtime.getRuntime().exec(taskAction) at line 69. Dataflow: User-controlled serialized data is deserialized directly into the object state, and the 'taskAction' field is subsequently used in a system command execution sink. Sanitization: Although there is a length check and string prefix check, these do not prevent command injection (e.g., 'ping -c 1 127.0.0.1') if the attacker can bypass or manipulate the input. This is a classic insecure deserialization vulnerability leading to RCE.

title: datadog/java-sqli
message: Source: The 'accountName' parameter originated from the @RequestParam user input in the 'completed' method and was passed to 'injectableQuery'. Sink: The query string is constructed via concatenation and used in 'connection.prepareStatement' (line 48). Dataflow: The untrusted input 'accountName' is concatenated directly into 'queryString' on line 45, which is then passed to the sink on line 48 without any sanitization or parameterization. This is a clear SQL injection vulnerability as the code allows manipulation of the SQL statement structure.

title: datadog/java-xss
message: Source: The @CurrentUsername annotation provides the username. Sink: The File constructor on line 32 takes the username as part of the file path. Dataflow: The untrusted username flows directly into the file path construction without validation. Sanitization: No sanitization is performed on the username. An attacker who can control their assigned username (e.g., via registration inputs) can use characters like '..' to perform a path traversal attack and write/overwrite files outside the intended directory. This is a path traversal vulnerability.

title: datadog/java-xss
message: The code accepts a userId parameter directly from user input and passes it to the verification logic without validating whether the provided userId belongs to the currently authenticated session or if the security questions are correctly linked to that specific userId. Source: 'userId' request parameter. Sink: 'verificationHelper.verifyAccount' method call at line 58. Dataflow: User-controlled input flows unsanitized into a logic check that determines authentication success. This represents a lack of proper authorization control leading to potential account verification bypass.

title: datadog/java-sqli
message: Source: User-supplied parameters 'username_login' and 'password_login' from @RequestParam. Sink: 'connection.prepareStatement' on line 44. Dataflow: Untrusted input is directly concatenated into the SQL statement string. Sanitization: None. The use of string concatenation to build a query instead of using parameterized queries (placeholders) allows for SQL Injection. Conclusion: Matches SQL Injection vulnerability, confirmed.

title: datadog/java-xss
message: Source: The 'commentStr' parameter in 'createNewComment'. Sink: The 'comments.add(comment)' call at line 83 which persists user-provided input without sanitization. Dataflow: Data is parsed from JSON and added to the 'userComments' map at line 84, then retrieved and returned in 'retrieveComments' to be rendered by the front-end. No sanitization is performed on user input. This is a intentional Stored XSS vulnerability in the context of the WebGoat training application.

title: datadog/java-xss
message: Source: multipartFile.getOriginalFilename() provides the untrusted filename from the user. Sink: destinationDir.toPath().resolve(...) at line 75, followed by Files.copy. Dataflow: The user-provided filename is joined with a base directory without path normalization or sanitization, allowing path traversal (e.g., passing '..\/..\/file.txt'). No sanitization is performed on the filename before using it in resolve(). Conclusion: This is a confirmed path traversal vulnerability.

title: datadog/java-xss
message: Source: The HTTP request method obtained via request.getMethod(). Sink: The conditional check at line 46 that restricts access based on the HTTP verb. Dataflow: The method checks if the request is a 'GET' request to block access. However, because the endpoint is mapped with @GetMapping to the same path, and standard Spring MVC request handling will prioritize the explicit routing, this specific implementation attempts to use VERB-based filtering manually.
